title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
subtitle: Preventing lost updates and double-booking in high-concurrency reservation and inventory systems.
keyTakeaways: Pessimistic locking acquires exclusive row locks (`SELECT . FOR UPDATE`) upfront before modifying data, serializing contending transactions.
Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) uses a `version` column or compare-and-swap (CAS) check at write time without holding database locks.
Choose Pessimistic locking when contention is high and rollbacks are expensive; choose Optimistic locking when contention is low or reads span user think-time.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely and blocks concurrent writers immediately using `SELECT . FOR UPDATE`. While effective for short, high-contention server-side transactions (such as deducting flash-sale inventory), holding exclusive locks across multiple rows can trigger deadlocks if two transactions acquire locks in opposite orders.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Pessimistic locking acquires exclusive row locks (`SELECT . FOR UPDATE`) upfront before modifying data, serializing contending transactions.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) uses a `version` column or compare-and-swap (CAS) check at write time without holding database locks.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking:
bullets: **Optimistic Locking (Version / CAS)**: Provides no database locks held during reads; immune to deadlocks; scales well when conflicts are rare. Best suited for Low-to-medium contention updates, HTTP ETag APIs, and multi-step UI workflows.

**Pessimistic Locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE)**: Guarantees progress without wasted retries under high contention; supports `skip locked`. Best suited for High-contention inventory allocation, wallet transfers, and worker queue claiming.
Consistent Lock Ordering: Always sort entity IDs ascending (`ORDER BY account_id ASC`) before running `SELECT . FOR UPDATE` on multiple rows to mathematically prevent circular wait deadlocks.
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`: Crucial pattern for database-backed job queues or ticket allocation where workers grab the next available unlocked item without waiting.
Safe Across User Think-Time: Essential for collaborative wiki editing or e-commerce checkout forms where a user views a page for 30 seconds before submitting.
High Contention Collapse: If 500 users try to update the exact same hot row simultaneously under OCC, 499 will fail and retry in a storm, wasting CPU.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Low-to-medium contention updates, HTTP ETag APIs, and multi-step UI workflows, suited for environments requiring No database locks held during reads; immune to deadlocks; scales well when conflicts are rare.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for High-contention inventory allocation, wallet transfers, and worker queue claiming, where Guarantees progress without wasted retries under high contention; supports `SKIP LOCKED`.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Optimistic locking never holds a database lock while reading or computing. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: high retry overhead and wasted work under heavy contention on hot rows.
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: reduces concurrency, holds connections longer, and introduces deadlock risks.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Choose Pessimistic locking when contention is high and rollbacks are expensive; choose Optimistic locking when contention is low or reads span user think-time.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: In Ticketmaster or Hotel Booking interviews, propose `SELECT . FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` when picking from a pool of interchangeable items, or Optimistic Locking (`version = version + 1`) when users pick a specific seat map item.
